newsitem.title: USA: US spot natgas drifts lower ahead of cool weather.
newsitem.headline: US spot natgas drifts lower ahead of cool weather.

text.p: U.S. spot natural gas prices drifted lower Thursday as cooler weather was expected to blanket most of the U.S. this weekend and into early next week, industry sources said.
Louisiana Gulf Coast prices at the Henry Hub on average slipped one cent to $2.13-2.15 per mmBtu, with the lower-priced deals reported done shortly before nomination deadlines.
Similarly in south Texas prices fell one to two cents to about $2.06-2.08.
In west Texas, Permian prices erased Wednesday's gains, falling back to about $1.95-1.97, while Waha was quoted at $1.99-2.04.
Southern California prices also softened slightly to about $2.12.
Warmer weather is expected to return to the Southwest Monday and continue through Wednesday, Weather Services Corp (WSC) reported.
In the Northeast, where forecasted thunderstorms were expected to push temperatures back into the low-80s F, New York city gate prices slipped into the high-$2.30s, traders said.
In the Midwest, prices eased by about three cents to the high-$1.90s, with Chicago city-gate quoted at $2.17-2.18.

Temperatures in the region are forecast to drop to normal to slightly below-normal levels through the weekend, with readings in Chicago expected to fall to highs in the low-70s and high-60s F through the middle of next week, WSC reported.

Separately, American Gas Association said Wednesday that U.S. gas stocks rose last week by 91 bcf, at the low end of the 90-100 bcf expected range, and were still 220 bcf, or 21 percent, above year-ago.

Eastern storage, which gained 59 bcf last week, was 104 bcf, or 20 percent, over last year. Producing region stocks rose 21 bcf and remained almost 60 percent above 1996 levels. Western inventories continued to lag year-ago by 14 percent.

Also, Mobil Corp said its Mary Ann gas processing plant, with a capacity of 380-390 million cubic feet per day, will likely be fully restored by this weekend. Planned work at the plant in Coden, Ala., began in mid-May.
